transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

My thoughts won’t slow down, and it’s gotten to the point where I can’t focus enough to do my work safely. I'm a pipefitter apprentice, and they actually had to pause my training because it's just not safe for me to be on the site like this.
Have you struggled with these racing thoughts and focus issues since childhood, or is this a relatively new change from how you normally feel?

No, this isn't something I've dealt with since childhood—it's a pretty recent change. This whole rollercoaster of highs and crashes started about five months ago when we got put on the big Miami project, though I've been feeling the heavier, down periods for about nine months now.
During those "down periods" you mentioned, did you have times lasting at least two weeks where you felt consistently sad, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or had very low energy?

Yes, those down periods have lasted way longer than two weeks—it's been a solid nine months of feeling heavy, drained, and completely unlike myself. During those times, I completely lose interest in things I used to love, like learning new torch tricks or helping the kids at the community center, and I'll just stare at my tools or my phone for hours.
During those "high" periods you mentioned, did you experience a significantly decreased need for sleep—like feeling fully rested after only a few hours—or feel unusually energetic and active?

Yes, I get incredibly energetic and feel like I can't stop moving, to the point where I'll volunteer for double shifts, reorganize my apartment at midnight, and take on multiple projects. But I don't feel peacefully rested; instead, I just lie awake until three or four in the morning with my brain buzzing because I feel like I have to do ten things at once.
You mentioned having down periods for about nine months. Did these low, heavy periods occur as a distinct phase that was completely separate from your high, energetic periods?

The heavy, down feelings have been a constant presence for about nine months, but the high, energetic rollercoaster only started five months ago. Since then, they haven't really been separate; they've been mixed together, and I can swing from feeling on top of the world to crashing down in the exact same afternoon.
During those high-energy times, did you feel unusually confident, like you had special abilities, or did you find yourself doing risky things that you would normally avoid?

Yes, during those high periods I felt incredibly confident, like I was the only one on the crew who truly understood the water system we were installing and could redesign the whole thing to get featured in a magazine. I also did some risky things, like climbing up to snap selfies on the scaffold at 2 a.m. because I felt so on top of the world.
When you are experiencing those high-energy, buzzing feelings, do you also feel deeply sad, hopeless, or down at the exact same time?

No, they don't really happen at the exact same moment. I tend to swing back and forth, going from feeling on top of the world to irritable and angry in the same afternoon, while the heavy, hopeless feelings are usually their own long, separate phase.
During these high-energy times, have you ever heard voices or seen things that others couldn't, or believed things that others insisted were not real?

No, I've never had those kinds of experiences like hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there. While I've felt extremely confident and had really big ideas during my high periods, I've never believed things that were completely detached from reality.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a history of a depressive episode lasting nine months, followed by a current manic episode of five months' duration. Symptoms of the current manic episode include racing thoughts, increased energy and activity, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, and risky behavior (climbing scaffolding at 2 a.m.). These symptoms have resulted in significant functional impairment, leading to suspension from his pipefitter apprentice training. He denies any psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions. This clinical picture meets the criteria for Bipolar Affective Disorder, current episode manic without psychotic symptoms (F31.1).
